meta.title: Security and Quality Audit
meta.app: Chairside - salon and barbershop booking app
meta.subtitle: Findings, business impact, and remediation
meta.coverLabel: Sample report - published as a portfolio example

executiveSummary.intro: This report reviews a salon and barbershop booking app in two parts: whether every feature works the way it was asked for (functional review), and whether it is secure. It documents the fixes applied and is written for the business owner: each finding explains what was found, why it matters for the business, and what was done about it.
executiveSummary.foundationNote: The app is built on solid foundations. The database keeps each salon's data separate, visitors cannot read the tables directly, and the system already prevents two bookings landing on the same person at the same time. The automated security scan offered by the build platform reported no issues at the time of the audit (October 2026); that same report notes it cannot catch every possible risk.
executiveSummary.theme: The issues found are subtler than missing basics: the booking and permission rules were enforced only in the app's screens, not on the server. Anyone who talks to the system directly, bypassing the screens, could do things the screens never allow. That is the thread running through the most serious findings.
executiveSummary.outcome: Of 24 findings (19 from the security review, 5 from the functional review), the 2 High and most Medium issues are fixed or materially reduced; the rest are documented with clear recommendations. Every fix is backed by an automated test that failed before the change and passes after it. Of the 19 requirements in the original request, 15 are now met, 4 partly and none missed. The original app is preserved unchanged for before-and-after comparison.
executiveSummary.testRun: Latest test run (2026-10-13): 55 tests: 50 passed, 1 skipped (an environment-dependent time-zone demonstration), 4 recorded as to-do (functional items left as recommendations).
topRisks: A stranger who knew a client's phone number could change that client's name and email.
A single visitor could flood the booking calendar and client list with fake entries and make it unusable.
Any staff member could delete a client and that client's entire history.
Bookings could be created at closed times (03:00, closed days, or years ahead) by bypassing the app.
Typing someone's email into the staff list could silently give them access to your client data.
Stylists could miss appointments: the calendar hid appointments outside opening hours, and a stylist saw only part of a client's history, so the AI briefing and reminder were built from partial data.

severityRubric.meaning: An anonymous, unauthenticated attacker can read or alter data across salons, or take over accounts, with little effort.

An anonymous or low-privilege caller, by talking to the system directly, can read or change another party's personal data, or deny a core business function such as the booking calendar - with no insider help.
Needs a valid account, a specific piece of knowledge, or an insider step; or the damage is recoverable; or it is an extra layer of defence that only matters if another flaw is also present.
Limited or hard-to-reach impact, or a good-practice, hygiene or maintainability gap.
No practical security impact; recorded for completeness.

designDecisions: Owners and staff can place, move or cancel appointments outside published opening hours and on closed days. This is a deliberate product choice for this app: salons routinely take off-hours or day-off appointments, so booking management inside the app keeps full control of the calendar. The public booking page that clients use is still held to the opening-hours, open-day and 21-day advance rules (see BH-01), and the system still prevents two appointments from overlapping on any path.

requirements.intro: Each sentence of the original request was checked against the app, by automated tests or by step-by-step manual checks on a local copy. Long sentences were split into their parts, giving 19 requirements.

rows.sentence: Build me a booking app for hair salons and barbershops.
Any salon owner should be able to sign up, create their salon, add their staff and their services with prices and durations.
rows.findings: FN-05 (services and staff cannot be edited)

rows.sentence: Each salon gets its own public booking page where customers pick a service, a staff member and a free time slot, and book with their name, phone number and email.
Staff log in and see their own calendar for the day and week.
The owner sees all bookings, can cancel or move them, and has a dashboard with revenue per week and the most popular services.
Owners and staff can keep notes on each customer (preferences, past services, anything useful).

Add an AI button on the customer page that summarises the customer's history and notes before their appointment, and an AI button that writes a friendly reminder message we can send by WhatsApp or SMS.
Make it modern, clean and mobile friendly.
rows.findings: Checked at phone width (375 px) on every main screen

requirements.summary: 19 requirements: 15 met, 4 partly met, 0 missed (before the two functional fixes: 12 met, 7 partly met).

strengths: Each salon's data is isolated from every other salon's (verified by tests).
Anonymous visitors cannot read database tables directly; public actions go only through a small set of controlled functions.
Double-booking the same staff member at the same time is prevented by the database itself.
Prices on past bookings are snapshotted, so later price changes do not rewrite history.
The powerful server key never reaches the browser.
The AI features run as the signed-in user, so they cannot reach another salon's clients.

findings.title: A visitor could change an existing client's name and email
findings.found: The public booking flow identified clients by phone number. A booking made with an existing client's phone number overwrote that client's stored name and email with whatever was typed.
findings.impact: Anyone who knew (or guessed) a client's phone number could rename that client and change their email, and the new booking attached to that client's history and notes. This corrupts the client list and could be used to impersonate or harass a client.
findings.whatChanged: We changed the rule that saves a client from a public booking so it never overwrites a client who already exists: it keeps the stored name and email and only fills in blanks. We also added a field that records the name typed at booking time and show it to staff on the client screen when it differs, so they can check it is the same person.
findings.howVerified: Test '[#1]' in public-booking.test.ts and http-e2e.test.ts failed on the original app (the client's name was overwritten) and passes after the change (the stored name is unchanged).
findings.whatRemains: A stranger who knows a client's phone number can still attach a booking to that client's record without changing it. Closing this fully needs a one-time code sent to the phone at booking time.

findings.title: No limit on public bookings
findings.found: A single anonymous visitor could create an unlimited number of bookings; there was no rate limit or quota.
findings.impact: An attacker could fill the calendar and client table with fake entries and make the system unusable for the salon.
findings.whatChanged: We added two limits to the booking function: at most 5 upcoming bookings per phone number, and at most 10 bookings per salon per minute.
findings.howVerified: Two tests in public-booking.test.ts (the per-phone cap and the per-salon burst) accepted the flood before and stop it after.
findings.whatRemains: Per-visitor rate limiting and a CAPTCHA need a layer in front of the app (the booking call comes straight from the browser), and the AI features still need a per-user usage limit.

findings.title: Bookings could be made at impossible times
findings.found: The rules about opening hours, open days and how far ahead clients may book existed only in the app's screens. Calling the booking service directly, the only server check was that the time was not in the past.
findings.impact: Someone bypassing the app could create appointments while the salon is closed, outside opening hours, or years in the future. The public calendar stops reflecting reality and staff cannot trust it.
findings.whatChanged: We added the booking rules to the server function that creates a public booking: it now checks the salon's open days, opening hours, a 21-day limit, and that the chosen time lands on a valid 15-minute slot, all judged in the salon's own time zone. We also added a time-zone setting to each salon so the checks use the right clock.
findings.designNote: These rules apply to the public booking page only. When the owner or staff create or move a booking inside the signed-in app, they are deliberately allowed to book outside opening hours and on closed days (see Design decisions). Overlap is still prevented on every path.
findings.howVerified: Tests '[#2] 03:00', '[#2] years in the future', '[#2] closed day' and '[BH-01] 15-minute grid' in public-booking.test.ts were accepted on the original app and are rejected after the change.

findings.title: Staff could do more than their role should allow
findings.found: Any staff member could edit and delete client records, and could read every booking in the salon. Deleting a client also deleted that client's entire booking and note history.
findings.impact: A single stylist could wipe a client's whole history, or browse other staff members' clients - well beyond 'see your own calendar'.
findings.whatChanged: We changed the database access rules: staff may read clients (needed to keep notes), but only the owner may add, change or delete them; and each staff member can read only the bookings assigned to them, while the owner reads all.
findings.howVerified: Tests in role-matrix.test.ts and http-e2e.test.ts show staff can no longer edit or delete clients, and a test in pentest.test.ts shows a staff member sees only their own bookings. All failed before and pass after.
findings.whatRemains: Staff can still read the salon's whole client list (names, phone, email, notes), because they need it to keep notes; only their booking view is limited to their own. Restricting the client list per staff member would be a separate product decision. Owners can also still delete a client (which removes that client's history); a soft-delete that hides instead of erasing is recommended. This change also limited the client history staff saw on the client page and in the AI buttons; the functional review caught that and it was fixed as FN-01.

findings.title: Staff invitations joined people without consent
findings.found: Adding an email address to the staff list silently linked that person to the salon the next time they signed in, with no acceptance step.
findings.impact: A person could be given access to a salon's client data without ever agreeing to join, and the behaviour was unpredictable when an email belonged to more than one salon.
findings.whatChanged: We removed the automatic linking on sign-in and added an explicit invitation: the invited person sees a pending invite and must click Accept, and only an invite addressed to their own email can be accepted.
findings.howVerified: Tests in pentest.test.ts confirm sign-in no longer auto-joins, a different email cannot accept the invite, and the invited person can accept their own.

findings.title: No limits on booking form input
findings.found: The booking form accepted names, phone numbers and emails of unlimited length and with no format checking (a 20,000-character name was accepted).
findings.impact: Oversized or malformed data could break staff screens and outgoing messages and bloat the database.
findings.whatChanged: We added length and basic format checks to the booking function for the name, phone number and email.
findings.howVerified: Test '[#2/SEC-02] name length' in public-booking.test.ts accepted a 20,000-character name before and rejects it after.

findings.title: Missing security headers
findings.found: The app sent none of the standard browser security headers (such as a content security policy or anti-framing header).
findings.impact: The site could be embedded invisibly in a malicious page to trick clients (clickjacking), and browser defences against injected scripts were weaker than they should be.
findings.whatChanged: We added a content security policy and the other standard security headers to every server response, and allowed the specific resources the app actually needs so nothing breaks.
findings.howVerified: Test in security-headers.test.ts checks the headers are present, and a live check confirmed the booking and sign-in pages load with no policy violations.
findings.whatRemains: The policy still permits inline scripts (it has to, because the app's framework injects them as the page loads), which weakens its protection against injected scripts. Tightening it to a stricter, nonce-based policy is a recommended follow-up (see the roadmap).

findings.title: Login session stored in the browser
findings.found: The login session token is kept in the browser's local storage.
findings.impact: If a script-injection flaw ever occurred, an attacker could read the session and take over the account.
howToFix: Store the login session in a secure, HttpOnly cookie so page scripts cannot read it.
Keep the content security policy added in SEC-05 in place as an added layer.

findings.title: Personal data handling and the AI features
findings.found: Client personal data (name, phone, email, notes, visit history) is sent to an outside AI provider for the summary and reminder features. There was no stated retention period, no deletion or export path, and no privacy notice on the booking page.
findings.impact: Clients' personal data leaves the salon's system with no stated handling, and the salon cannot easily honour a request to delete someone's data.
findings.whatChanged: So far only one thing has changed: a short privacy notice was added to the public booking page, telling clients their details are shared only with the salon and how to ask for changes or deletion. The substantive data-protection work below is still outstanding.
findings.whatRemains: Define a retention period with automatic deletion, add a way to export or erase a client's data on request, and reduce how much client data is sent to the AI.

findings.title: Business rules lived only in the app screens
findings.found: Opening hours, the booking window, cancel and move rules and revenue all lived in the browser, not on the server.
findings.impact: Anyone bypassing the app screens could ignore the salon's rules.
findings.whatChanged: The rules for public (client-facing) bookings were moved onto the server function and into the database access rules, so they hold even when the app screens are bypassed.
findings.designNote: Owner and staff booking management (create, move, cancel) is intentionally left to the signed-in app and is not server-constrained to opening hours (see Design decisions).
findings.howVerified: Covered by the BH-01 and SEC-03 tests, which exercise the public rules on the server.
findings.whatRemains: Revenue and popular-services totals are still added up in the browser rather than on the server; that is tracked separately as SE-03.

findings.title: Time slots used the visitor's time zone
findings.found: The list of free time slots was calculated using the visitor's device time zone, while the salon's opening hours are stored without a time zone.
findings.impact: A client in another region saw shifted times and could book a slot that is not actually open at the salon; two clients in different regions picking the same time sent two different real times.
findings.whatChanged: We compute the available time slots in the salon's time zone instead of the visitor's, and pass the salon's time zone through to the booking page.
findings.howVerified: Test in timezone.test.ts passes in three different time zones (it produced shifted times before the change).
findings.whatRemains: Found in the functional review: the public page still asks for busy times over the visitor's own day, so for a visitor far east of the salon an evening slot can show as free and is then refused by the server (no double booking is possible). Calendar days and AI message times also follow the device or a fixed zone rather than the salon's. Recommended (roadmap).

findings.title: Lists and dashboard will under-report at scale
findings.found: Lists and the dashboard have no paging and silently stop at the first 1000 rows; revenue is added up in the browser.
findings.impact: As the salon grows, the dashboard and lists will quietly show incomplete or wrong totals.
howToFix: Calculate revenue and popular services on the server rather than in the browser.
Add paging to the client and booking lists so nothing is cut off at 1000 rows.

findings.title: Data model: phone duplicates and no audit trail
findings.found: Clients are identified by phone number with no normalisation (so '+90...', '0...' and spaced variants could create duplicates), deletes cascade, and there is no record of who changed what.
findings.impact: The same client entered two ways becomes two records, and deletions remove history with no audit trail.
findings.whatChanged: We normalise phone numbers to one format before saving, so the same client typed different ways becomes a single record.
findings.howVerified: Test '[Item 12]' in public-booking.test.ts confirms two formats of the same number map to one client.
findings.whatRemains: Switch deletes to soft-delete (hide rather than erase) and add an audit trail of who changed what and when.

findings.title: Staff saw only part of a client's history
findings.found: This problem was caused by one of this audit's own security fixes, not by the original app, and the functional review caught it. After staff were limited to their own calendar (SEC-03), the client page and both AI buttons read the same limited data. A stylist opening a client saw "Visits 0" and no past visits, even when the client had visits with colleagues.
findings.impact: A stylist preparing for an appointment saw an empty history; the AI briefing summarised only their own visits; the AI reminder could tell a client they had no upcoming appointment and invite them to book again, although they already had one with a colleague.
findings.whatChanged: We added a controlled way to read one client's full history for anyone who works at that client's salon, with prices shown only to the owner. The client page and both AI buttons now use it. Staff still see only their own appointments in the calendar.
findings.howVerified: Tests '[FN-01]' in functional.test.ts failed before the change and pass after it (staff see every visit without prices; the owner sees prices; another salon, an outsider and anonymous visitors get nothing). Checked in the running app: the stylist now sees all four appointments.

findings.title: The calendar hid appointments outside opening hours
findings.found: The day calendar drew only the current opening hours. An appointment before opening or after closing, for example after the owner shortened the hours, was drawn outside the visible grid.
findings.impact: A stylist looking at the day calendar could miss an appointment entirely.
findings.whatChanged: The calendar grid now widens to include any appointment outside the opening hours.
findings.howVerified: Tests '[FN-02]' in functional.test.ts failed before the change and pass after it. Checked in the running app: a 09:00 appointment with opening hours from 10:00 is now visible.

findings.title: Booking-link not cleaned on the server
findings.found: A salon's public booking-link (slug) was not sanitised when set directly through the service, bypassing the app's cleanup.
findings.impact: Broken or confusing public booking links.
findings.whatChanged: We clean the salon booking-link on the server and enforce a safe format, and reject negative prices as part of the same hardening.
findings.howVerified: Tests in pentest.test.ts confirm a malformed link is normalised and a negative price is rejected.

findings.title: AI reminder could be steered by note content
findings.found: Client name and notes flow directly into the AI prompt, and the AI-written reminder is sent from the salon's own phone number.
findings.impact: Someone could try to steer the reminder message (for example to insert a link) by writing instructions into a client's note or name.
findings.whatChanged: We wrap the client's name and notes as data (clearly marked as not instructions) before sending them to the AI, and strip any links out of the reminder before it can be sent.
findings.howVerified: Test in ai-sanitize.test.ts removes a link smuggled into a simulated AI reply and keeps normal text. No live exploit was attempted against the production model, which is not reachable in this test setup.
findings.whatRemains: The hard control here is stripping links from the outgoing message. Wrapping the notes as data reduces, but cannot fully guarantee against, an AI model being steered; this is why the status is 'Mitigated' rather than 'Fixed'. Keep untrusted text out of the instruction part of the prompt as the AI model changes.

findings.title: Environment file in the repository; dependency advisories
findings.found: An environment file was committed to the generated project (it contained only the public key), and there are development-only dependency advisories.
findings.impact: Low: the committed key is public by design, and the advisories affect only the development tools, not the live app.
howToFix: Remove environment files from the repository and load secrets from the environment instead.
Update the development tool flagged by the dependency check.

findings.title: Password-guessing was not rate-limited (test project)
findings.found: Password strength, email confirmation and protection against revealing which emails are registered were all in good shape. However, repeated wrong-password attempts were not throttled in the test project.
findings.impact: Without a limit, automated password-guessing against an account is easier.
howToFix: Confirm the production password and sign-in settings.
Enable a limit or a temporary lockout after repeated failed sign-in attempts.

findings.title: Thin automated tests; some loosely-typed code
findings.found: The generated app shipped with a single automated test and some loosely-typed code.
findings.impact: Lower confidence that future changes will not quietly break something.
howToFix: Add automated tests that cover the main booking and account flows.
Replace loosely-typed code with explicit types.
Use the security test suite added by this audit as a starting point.

findings.title: Dashboard figures include appointments that have not happened
findings.found: "Revenue this week" adds every booked appointment of the week, including ones still to come, and there is no "completed" or "no-show" status. "Most popular services, last 8 weeks" also counts the next two weeks.
findings.impact: Booked value can be mistaken for earned revenue, and the ranking mixes in future bookings.
howToFix: Count only appointments that have taken place, or label the figure as booked revenue.
Limit the popular-services ranking to past appointments.
Add a completed / no-show status so revenue reflects what actually happened.

findings.title: The Bookings list does not reach every booking
findings.found: The Bookings screen shows only 60 days back and 90 days ahead; anything outside that window appears only in the calendar.
findings.impact: The owner cannot find older or far-ahead bookings in the list.
howToFix: Add paging or a date picker to the Bookings list (together with the server-side paging in SE-03).

findings.title: Services and staff cannot be edited
findings.found: Settings can add, switch off or delete a service, and add or switch off a staff member, but cannot change a price, a duration, a name or an email.
findings.impact: Raising a price means deleting the service and adding it again (past bookings keep their price, so history is safe).
howToFix: Add an edit form for services (name, price, duration) and staff (name, email).

findings.title: Internal helper functions callable by anyone
findings.found: Two internal helper functions could be called by anonymous visitors (harmless: they return nothing useful to an anonymous caller).
findings.impact: No practical impact; addressed as defence in depth.
findings.whatChanged: We removed anonymous access to the two helper functions, leaving them available only to signed-in users.
findings.howVerified: Test in pentest.test.ts confirms an anonymous caller can no longer run the helper.

hardening: Anonymous visitors had database-level table privileges by default, leaving the access rules as the only line of defence; those privileges were removed, so anonymous visitors can now use only the controlled public functions.
Phone numbers are normalised to one format so the same client is not stored twice.

roadmap.item: Move the login session to a secure, script-inaccessible cookie
Server-side totals and paging for lists and the dashboard
Data retention, deletion and export; minimise data sent to the AI
Per-visitor rate limiting and a CAPTCHA at the edge; AI usage limit
Confirm production auth settings and enable password-guessing protection
Keep environment files out of the repository; update development tools
Broaden automated tests; tighten types; soft-delete and audit trail
Tighten the content security policy to a nonce-based one that no longer allows inline scripts
Dashboard counts only appointments that took place; paging on the Bookings list; edit forms for services and staff
Use the salon's time zone for busy times, calendar days and AI messages

scope: Testing was limited to a locally running copy of the app and a separate test project with the same database structure applied to it. No hosted or production environment was accessed. All test data is fictitious.

reproduce.intro: The findings are backed by an automated test suite. To re-run it against your own test project, provide connection details in a local environment file (not included in this report) with these variable names:
envVars: AUDIT_GEMINI_API_KEY (only for the AI prompt-injection test)
steps: Run the test suite. With only the original structure applied, the finding tests fail (proving the issue); with migrations 0001 and 0002 applied, they pass (proving the fix).
